mainTopic: How a שומר who chooses to pay earns the thief's double payment (כפל): רבא's mechanism, רבי יוחנן on 'saying I will pay', and רב פפא on different guards
overview: The משנה taught that a שומר who pays the owner for a stolen animal, instead of swearing, gets the thief's double payment (כפל). The גמרא asks how the owner can give away something that may never exist. רבא answers that the owner transfers the cow itself to the שומר, either from the time of the deposit or, in a second version, right before the theft. רבי זירא objects to the first version because of the fleece and offspring, and the גמרא explains the practical differences between רבא's two versions. Next, רבי יוחנן rules that the משנה's word 'paid' only means the שומר said 'I will pay', and a ברייתא about a renter supports him. רב פפא explains which guards earn the כפל by admitting they must pay, and the two versions of his statement disagree about a borrower. רב זביד, quoting אביי, says a borrower must actually pay, and a ברייתא using the word 'went ahead' (קידם) seems to support him. The reciters confirm that the two ברייתות were taught together, so the difference in wording counts. Finally the גמרא begins to discuss a שומר who changes his mind about paying, and this continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The double payment may never come into existence
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its challenge: the כפל is a very uncertain thing. The animal may never be stolen, the thief may never be found, and he may confess and be exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: Who says the animal will be stolen? Even if it is stolen, who says the thief will be found? Even if he is found, who says he will pay double? Maybe he will confess and be exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing a challenge against the משנה. It shows that the double payment the שומר is supposed to get is a far-off thing that may never exist.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Normally a person cannot give away a דבר שלא בא לעולם, something not yet in existence. The גמרא lists three layers of doubt: theft, catching the thief, and actually paying. The last doubt is that a thief who confesses before witnesses come is exempt from כפל, because כפל is a fine.

keyTerms.meaning: Who can say? (meaning: it is not at all certain)
He confesses and is exempt (from the double payment)
Even if you say / even if you grant

phrases.english: Who can say that it will be stolen?
And even if you say that it will be stolen,
who can say that the thief will be found?
And even if the thief is found,
who can say that he will pay?
Perhaps he will confess and be exempt!
phrases.notes: A thief who admits on his own, before witnesses come, does not pay the extra double. He only returns what he took.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the challenge to the משנה that began before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that a שומר who pays gets the כפל
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The כפל is a דבר שלא בא לעולם, so it cannot be transferred.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole sugya: every answer below is a way around the problem of transferring something that does not exist yet.

steps.title: רבא: The cow itself is transferred retroactively
steps.stepSummary: רבא answers that the owner is treated as if he transferred the cow itself to the שומר from the time of the deposit, on condition that it is stolen and the שומר pays.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: It is as if the owner told him, 'When it is stolen, and you choose to pay me, my cow is yours from right now.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא answers the challenge. The owner is not giving away the future כפל. He is giving away the cow, which already exists.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The cow is something that exists, so it can be transferred with a condition. The condition is theft plus the שומר choosing to pay. Once that happens, the cow belongs to the שומר going back to the start (מעכשיו), so the כפל that comes from it is automatically his.

keyTerms.meaning: It is considered as though he said to him
From now (backdated to the time of the deposit)

phrases.english: Rava said: It is as though he said to him:
phrases.notes: "He" is the owner, speaking to the שומר when he handed over the animal.

phrases.english: When it is stolen, and you want to, and you pay me,
my cow is hereby acquired by you from now.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reframing what is transferred: the existing cow instead of the future payment
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner was transferring the כפל itself, which does not exist yet.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner transfers the cow retroactively on a condition, and the כפל comes along with it.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think the owner gives away the double payment directly. He gives away the cow, and the double payment comes with the cow.

steps.title: רבי זירא: Then the fleece and offspring should also go to the שומר
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא objects: if the cow belonged to the שומר from the start, its wool and calves should be his too, but a ברייתא says they are not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי זירא objected: If so, even its fleece and offspring should go to him! Why was it taught 'except for its fleece and offspring'?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא attacks רבא's answer by pointing out a result that clashes with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the cow was the שומר's from the time of the deposit, anything that grew from it in the meantime, wool and babies, should also be his. But a ברייתא clearly leaves those out. So רבא's version proves too much.

keyTerms.meaning: Why then was it taught (in a ברייתא)?

phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira objects to it:

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, אֲפִילּוּ גִּיזּוֹתֶיהָ וּוַלְדוֹתֶיהָ נָמֵי!
phrases.english: If so, even its fleece and its offspring too should be his!
Why then is it taught: except for its fleece and its offspring?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא: אִי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבא's answer from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's claim that the cow is transferred מעכשיו
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A full retroactive transfer would give the שומר the fleece and offspring too, which contradicts the ברייתא.

steps.title: רבי זירא: The transfer leaves out the fleece and offspring
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא fixes רבא's idea: the owner transfers the cow retroactively, but keeps the fleece and offspring for himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבי זירא said: It is as if the owner told him, 'except for its fleece and offspring.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא keeps רבא's basic idea but adds an exception to fit the ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner still transfers the cow retroactively, so the כפל goes to the שומר. But the owner is treated as if he said, 'not including the wool and the calves.' This matches the ברייתא exactly.

phrases.english: Rather, Rabbi Zeira said:
It is as though he said to him:
except for its fleece and its offspring.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves רבי זירא's own objection by refining רבא's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding an exception to the conditional transfer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The whole cow, with everything it produces, goes to the שומר.
steps.terutzMaskana: The cow goes to the שומר retroactively, except for its fleece and offspring.

steps.title: Why assume every owner makes this exception?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the ruling is stated as a fixed rule, as if every owner has this exact exception in mind.
steps.simpleTranslation: And why is it stated without any qualification?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short question about רבי זירא's answer, setting up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Not every owner actually says these words. So how can the ruling be stated as a fixed rule for everyone? The גמרא wants a reason why we assume all owners think this way.

keyTerms.meaning: Why is it stated flatly, as a fixed rule for every case?

phrases.english: And why is it stated without qualification?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the assumption behind רבי זירא's answer.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why we can assume every owner transfers the כפל but not the fleece and offspring.

steps.title: Outside profit people give away, body profit they keep
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that people usually give away profit that comes from outside, like the כפל, but keep profit that grows from the animal's body.
steps.simpleTranslation: Normally, a person tends to give away profit that comes from outside, but a person does not tend to give away profit that comes from the animal's own body.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers step 5 by explaining how people normally think.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The כפל comes from outside, from a thief, and is unexpected, so an owner does not mind giving it to a שומר who paid him. Wool and calves come from the animal itself and are expected, so an owner keeps them. That is why the rule can be stated for everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: The usual way of things / normally
A person tends to transfer (give away)

phrases.english: In the usual way of things,
profit that comes from outside,
phrases.notes: Like the double payment, which comes from the thief and not from the animal.

phrases.english: a person tends to transfer.
Profit that comes from its body,
a person does not tend to transfer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 5.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: People normally give away outside profit (כפל) but keep profit from the animal's body (fleece, offspring).
steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי זירא, the cow goes to the שומר retroactively, but not its fleece and offspring. People give away outside profit like the כפל, but keep profit from the animal's body.

steps.title: Second version of רבא: The cow is transferred just before the theft
steps.stepSummary: Some report רבא differently: the owner transfers the cow to the שומר right before the theft, not from the time of the deposit.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רבא said: It is as if the owner told him, 'When it is stolen, and you choose to pay me, it is yours from just before the theft.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a different report of what רבא said, with a new timing for the transfer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the cow becomes the שומר's סמוך לגניבתה, right before it is stolen, not מעכשיו. Since anything the cow produced before the theft was still the owner's, the fleece and offspring stay with him without any special exception. The כפל, which comes after the theft, still goes to the שומר.

phrases.english: Some say that Rava said:
It is as though he said to him:
When it is stolen, and you want to, and you pay me,
right before its theft it is acquired by you.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second version of רבא's answer to step 1, different from step 2.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The cow is transferred to the שומר right before the theft, so the כפל is his.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up the two versions of רבא. In the first, the transfer goes back to the deposit (מעכשיו). In the second, it happens only right before the theft (סמוך לגניבתה).

steps.title: What is the difference between the two versions?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the two versions of רבא: 'from now' (מעכשיו) and 'right before the theft' (סמוך לגניבתה).
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the difference between them?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up its next move by asking for a practical case where the two explanations would give different results.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both versions of רבא give the שומר the כפל. The first transfers the cow from the time of the deposit, and the second only right before the theft. The גמרא wants a real case where this difference matters. The next step answers this.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between them?

phrases.english: What is the difference between them?
phrases.notes: Between רבא's two versions: "yours from now" and "yours right before the theft."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares step 7 with the earlier explanation.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A practical case where the two explanations would lead to different outcomes.

steps.title: Two practical differences between the two versions
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא names two cases where the two versions of רבא lead to different results: רבי זירא's fleece and offspring question, and an animal standing in a marsh.
steps.simpleTranslation: There is a difference between them: the difficulty of רבי זירא. Or also: a case where the animal is standing in a marsh.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from Step 8. It gives two cases where the two versions of רבא's idea really lead to different results.
steps.deeperAnalysis: First difference: רבי זירא's problem about fleece and offspring only comes up if the cow is transferred from the time of the deposit. If the transfer happens only right before the theft, any wool or calves produced before then still belonged to the owner, so the problem never comes up. Second difference: if the animal was standing in a marsh when it was stolen, it was not in the שומר's area at that moment, so a transfer right before the theft would not work.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the two versions are not just two ways of saying the same thing. They lead to different results in real cases.

phrases.english: There is a difference between them: the difficulty of Rabbi Zeira.
phrases.notes: This is the fleece and offspring problem from Step 3. It only comes up if the transfer goes all the way back to the deposit.

phrases.english: Or also: where it is standing in a marsh.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 8 about the practical difference between the two versions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Two differences: (1) רבי זירא's fleece and offspring problem, which only applies if the transfer is from the time of the deposit; (2) an animal standing in a marsh at the time of the theft.

steps.title: Saying 'I will pay' is enough
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the משנה's word 'paid' does not mean actual payment. Once the שומר says 'I will pay,' he gains the rights.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה says: 'He paid and did not want to swear,' and so on. רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: 'Paid' does not mean he really paid. Rather, once he said 'I will pay,' it counts, even though he has not paid yet.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a line from the משנה and brings רבי יוחנן's explanation of the word 'paid.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה says that a שומר who paid instead of swearing gets the כפל when the thief is found. רבי יוחנן says the key moment is when the שומר commits to paying, not when the money actually changes hands. So a spoken commitment is enough to give him the right to the כפל.

keyTerms.meaning: I hereby will pay (a commitment to pay)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read 'שילם' in the משנה as actual payment. רבי יוחנן says a spoken commitment to pay is enough.

phrases.english: He paid and did not want to swear, etc.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yochanan said:
'Paid' does not mean he actually paid,
rather, once he said, 'I hereby will pay,'
even though he has not yet paid.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the meaning of 'paid' in the משנה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומר gains the right to the כפל as soon as he says 'I will pay,' even before he actually pays.

steps.title: The משנה's wording seems to require real payment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן: the משנה says 'paid,' which suggests that only actual payment counts.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in the משנה: 'He paid and did not want to swear.' If he paid, yes. If he did not pay, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן by reading the משנה's words closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה uses the word 'paid.' A plain reading suggests that without actual payment, the שומר does not get the כפל. That goes against רבי יוחנן's claim that saying 'I will pay' is enough.

phrases.english: We learned: He paid and did not want to swear.
If he paid, yes; if he did not pay, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's reading from Step 10.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's claim that saying 'I will pay' is enough.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Reading the first clause of the משנה closely: only one who actually 'paid' gets the כפל.

steps.title: The second half of the משנה points the other way
steps.stepSummary: The second half of the משנה suggests the opposite: just being willing to pay is enough. Since the two halves pull in opposite directions, no proof can be taken from this משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Look at the second half: 'He swore and did not want to pay.' The reason the owner gets the כפל is that the שומר did not want to pay. That means if he did want to pay, even though he did not pay yet, he would get it. So nothing can be learned from this משנה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge from Step 11 by reading the second half of the same משנה closely.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The second half stresses 'did not want' to pay. That suggests that wanting to pay would be enough. The first half seems to require real payment, while the second half seems to require only willingness. So the משנה gives no proof either way, and רבי יוחנן's view still stands.

keyTerms.meaning: Look at the second half (of the משנה)
Nothing can be learned from it

steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not proving רבי יוחנן right here. It is only showing that this משנה cannot be used against him.

phrases.english: Say the second half:
He swore and did not want to pay.
The reason is that he did not want to,

phrases.aramaic: הָא רָצָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא שִׁילֵּם.
phrases.english: but if he wanted to, even though he did not pay, he would get it.
Rather, nothing can be learned from this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Cancels out the inference from the first half of the משנה in Step 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects using the משנה as proof against רבי יוחנן.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The first half and the second half of the משנה point in opposite directions, so neither inference proves anything.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a renter who said 'I will pay and not swear' receives the כפל when the thief is found. This matches רבי יוחנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא supports רבי יוחנן: Someone rented a cow from another person and it was stolen. The renter said, 'I will pay and I will not swear.' Later the thief was found. The thief pays the כפל to the renter.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that agrees with רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the ברייתא, the renter only says 'I will pay.' Nothing is said about money changing hands, yet he still gets the כפל. That shows that a spoken commitment to pay is enough, just as רבי יוחנן said.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא was taught in agreement with him
Renter (a שומר who pays to use the item)
Double payment owed by a thief

steps.whatToRemember: According to רבי יוחנן, backed by the ברייתא, a שומר gets the right to the כפל the moment he says 'I will pay,' even before he actually pays.

phrases.english: It was taught in agreement with Rabbi Yochanan:
One who rents a cow from his friend, and it was stolen,
and that one said: 'I hereby will pay and I will not swear,'
and afterward the thief was found,
he pays the double payment to the renter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the משנה turned out to prove nothing (Step 12), a ברייתא gives clear support to רבי יוחנן.
steps.raayaObject: רבי יוחנן's rule that saying 'I will pay' is enough.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a renter who said 'I will pay and not swear' and received the כפל.

steps.title: Paid and unpaid guards gain the double payment by admitting they must pay
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא rules that a שומר חנם who admits negligence, and a שומר שכר who says the animal was stolen, receive the כפל. Each one could have freed himself with a different claim.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: An unpaid guard who says 'I was negligent' gets the double payment, because he could have freed himself by claiming theft. A paid guard who says 'It was stolen' gets the double payment, because he could have freed himself by claiming the animal broke a limb or died.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא explains why certain guards earn the right to the thief's double payment just by admitting they owe money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner gives the כפל to a guard who chose to take on payment when he had an easy way out. A שומר חנם is not liable for theft, so admitting negligence means he gave up that exemption. A שומר שכר is not liable for שבורה ומתה (accidents), so admitting theft means he gave up that exemption.

keyTerms.meaning: An unpaid guard. He pays only if he was negligent.
A paid guard. He pays for theft or loss, but not for accidents.
The owner transfers the double payment to him
The animal broke a limb or died (an accident beyond his control)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the key test for the rest of the discussion: a guard earns the כפל when his admission gives up a real, available exemption.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa says:
An unpaid guard, once he said: "I was negligent,"
[the owner] transfers the double payment to him,
since if he wanted, he could have freed himself with [a claim of] theft.
A paid guard, once he said: "It was stolen,"
[the owner] transfers the double payment to him,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאִי בָּעֵי פָּטַר נַפְשֵׁיהּ בִּשְׁבוּרָה וּמֵתָה.
phrases.english: since if he wanted, he could have freed himself with [a claim that it] broke a limb or died.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: שׁוֹמֵר חִנָּם, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאָמַר פָּשַׁעְתִּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on רבי יוחנן's rule that saying 'I will pay' is enough, and spells out what counts as 'saying it' for each type of guard.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומר חנם who admits negligence, and a שומר שכר who claims theft, gain the כפל, because each gave up an available exemption.

steps.title: A borrower who says 'I will pay' does not get the double payment
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא continues: a שואל who says 'I will pay' does not receive the כפל.
steps.simpleTranslation: A borrower who says 'I will pay' does not get the double payment.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא gives the opposite ruling for a borrower: his promise to pay does not earn him the כפל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A שואל is liable even for accidents, so his promise to pay seems to give up nothing. The next two steps explain this.

keyTerms.meaning: A borrower. He pays for almost everything, even accidents.

phrases.english: A borrower who says: "I hereby will pay" –
[the owner] does not transfer the double payment to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שׁוֹאֵל שֶׁאוֹמֵר הֲרֵינִי מְשַׁלֵּם לָא מַקְנֵי לֵיהּ כְּפֵילָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Contrasts the borrower with the two guards in step 14.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שואל does not gain the כפל just by saying he will pay.

steps.title: What exemption could a borrower ever have?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what claim a borrower could have used to free himself.
steps.simpleTranslation: With what could he have freed himself?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a question that sets up the reason for the borrower's different rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: By step 14's test, a guard earns the כפל by giving up an exemption. So we need to know whether a borrower has any real exemption to give up.

phrases.english: With what [claim] could he have freed himself?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind step 15.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a borrower has any available exemption that his promise to pay would give up.

steps.title: His only way out is rare, so he gives up nothing
steps.stepSummary: A borrower's only exemption is that the animal died from normal work, and that is uncommon.
steps.simpleTranslation: Only by claiming it died from the work. But dying from the work is not common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the borrower's only exemption, מתה מחמת מלאכה, almost never happens.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the borrower almost never has a real way out, his promise to pay does not give up anything. So the owner does not hand him the כפל for words alone.

keyTerms.meaning: The animal died because of the normal work it was borrowed for

phrases.english: With [a claim that] it died because of the work.
[But] dying because of the work is not common.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּמֵתָה מֵחֲמַת מְלָאכָה, מֵתָה מֵחֲמַת מְלָאכָה לָא שְׁכִיחַ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The borrower's only exemption, מתה מחמת מלאכה, is rare, so his promise to pay gives up nothing and does not earn the כפל.

steps.title: Second version: a borrower also gets the double payment
steps.stepSummary: Some report that רב פפא said a borrower who says 'I will pay' also receives the כפל, since he could have claimed מתה מחמת מלאכה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say רב פפא said: A borrower too, once he says 'I will pay,' gets the double payment, because if he wanted he could have freed himself by claiming the animal died from the work.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of רב פפא, which gives the borrower the same rule as the other guards.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, the borrower's exemption counts even though it is rare. So his promise to pay does give something up, and he earns the כפל.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix the two versions. In the first, the borrower does NOT get the כפל by words alone. In this second version, he does.

phrases.english: Some say [that] Rav Pappa said:
A borrower too, once he said: "I hereby will pay" –
[the owner] transfers the double payment to him,
since if he wanted, he could have freed himself
with [a claim that] it died because of the work.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא: שׁוֹאֵל נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the opposite version of רב פפא's ruling on a borrower from steps 15–17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שואל who says 'I will pay' gains the כפל, because he could have claimed מתה מחמת מלאכה.

steps.title: רב זביד quotes אביי: a borrower must actually pay
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד objects in the name of אביי that a borrower gets the כפל only after he actually pays, because he gets all the benefit from the loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said to him: This is what אביי said: A borrower gets it only once he actually pays. Why? Since all the benefit is his, the owner does not give him the double payment for words alone.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד challenges the second version of רב פפא by quoting אביי: words are not enough for a borrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The borrower uses the animal for free, so the owner feels no reason to be generous with him. The owner will give him the כפל only once he has actually paid, not for a promise.

keyTerms.meaning: Since all the benefit is his

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said to him:
This is what Abaye said:
A borrower – [only] once he actually pays.
What is the reason?
Since all the benefit is his,
[the owner] does not transfer the double payment to him through mere words.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב זְבִיד: הָכִי אָמַר אַבָּיֵי: שׁוֹאֵל עַד שֶׁיְּשַׁלֵּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Argues against the second version of רב פפא in step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second version of רב פפא, that a borrower gains the כפל by saying 'I will pay.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Quoting אביי: because the borrower gets all the benefit, the owner will not give him the כפל for words. He must actually pay.

steps.title: A ברייתא supports רב זביד
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that a borrower who went ahead and paid receives the כפל when the thief is found. This supports רב זביד.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא supports רב זביד: If someone borrowed a cow and it was stolen, and the borrower went ahead and paid, and later the thief was found, the thief pays the double payment to the borrower.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that matches רב זביד's view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא describes a borrower who actually paid, and only then gives him the כפל. This fits אביי's rule, quoted by רב זביד, that a borrower must actually pay.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא is taught that supports him
The double payment a thief owes

steps.whatToRemember: For a שומר חנם and a שומר שכר, admitting liability is enough to earn the כפל. For a שואל, the ברייתא supports רב זביד (in the name of אביי) that he must actually pay first.

phrases.english: It is taught [in a ברייתא] in line with Rav Zevid:
One who borrows a cow from his friend, and it was stolen,
and the borrower went ahead and paid,
and afterward the thief was found –
[the thief] pays the double payment to the borrower.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רב זביד's objection in step 19.
steps.raayaObject: רב זביד's view (in the name of אביי) that a borrower gains the כפל only after actually paying.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a borrower who went ahead and paid and then received the כפל when the thief was found.

steps.title: Is the ברייתא a refutation of רב פפא?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא fits the first version of רב פפא, but seems to refute the second version.
steps.simpleTranslation: According to the first version of רב פפא, this is certainly no refutation. According to the second version, shall we say it refutes him?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks how the ברייתא from the last step affects רב פפא. It asks whether it disproves the second version of his statement.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the first version, רב פפא required actual payment, which is exactly what the ברייתא says ('he went ahead and paid'). In the second version, he said that just saying 'I will pay' is enough. That seems to clash with a ברייתא that speaks of real payment.

keyTerms.meaning: the first version of a teaching
the later (second) version of a teaching
shall we say (introduces a suggestion the גמרא may reject)

phrases.english: According to the first version of Rav Pappa,
phrases.notes: That first version said the borrower gets the double payment only after he actually pays.

phrases.english: it is certainly not a refutation.
According to the latter version,
phrases.notes: This is the version from step 18: just saying 'I will pay' is enough.

phrases.english: shall we say it is a refutation of him?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the ברייתא from step 20 as a possible challenge against the second version of רב פפא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The second version of רב פפא (step 18)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא grants the כפל to a borrower who actually paid. That implies payment is required, against רב פפא's view that saying 'I will pay' is enough.

steps.title: The משנה also says 'paid' and we read it as 'said'
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא answers that the ברייתא is no stronger than the משנה, which says 'paid' yet was explained as 'said he would pay.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא could say to you: Is the ברייתא stronger than the משנה? The משנה teaches 'paid,' and we explained it as a case where he only said he would pay. Here too, the case is one where he said it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב פפא. It reads the ברייתא the same way the משנה was already read.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, the גמרא explained that the משנה's word 'paid' really means 'agreed to pay.' If the משנה can be read that way, the ברייתא can be too, so it is no proof that real payment is needed.

keyTerms.meaning: is it stronger? (is this source any more forceful?)
we established / we explained it as referring to
in a case where he said (he would pay)

phrases.english: Rav Pappa could say to you:
Is it stronger than our Mishnah?
which teaches 'he paid,'
and we established it as a case where he said he would pay;
here too, it is where he said it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְךָ רַב פָּפָּא מִי אַלִּימָא מִמַּתְנִיתִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 21.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the source by comparing it to the משנה
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא's 'paid' means actual payment, which refutes רב פפא.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Paid' can mean 'said he would pay,' just as in the משנה.

steps.title: The ברייתא says 'went ahead,' which the משנה does not
steps.stepSummary: The comparison is rejected: the ברייתא adds the word 'went ahead,' which points to actual payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: Are they comparable? There, in the משנה, it does not say 'went ahead.' Here, in the ברייתא, it does say 'went ahead'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on step 22. The ברייתא has an extra word that makes it harder to read as 'just said.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only says 'paid,' which leaves room for reinterpretation. The ברייתא says 'he went ahead (קידם) and paid.' That sounds like a real act of paying before the thief was found.

phrases.english: Are they comparable?
There it does not teach 'went ahead,'
here it teaches 'went ahead'!

steps.triggerLanguage: מִי דָּמֵי הָתָם לָא קָתָנֵי קִידֵּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the comparison made in step 22.
steps.kashyaTarget: The comparison between the ברייתא and the משנה
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The word 'קידם' in the ברייתא signals actual payment, so it cannot be reinterpreted like the משנה.

steps.title: 'Went ahead' means 'went ahead and said'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that 'went ahead' means he went ahead and declared he would pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'went ahead' mean? He went ahead and said he would pay.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב פפא again by explaining what the word 'went ahead' means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Went ahead' can describe speaking first. The borrower quickly announced 'I will pay' before the thief was found, so the word does not require real payment.

phrases.english: What is 'went ahead'?
He went ahead and said that he would pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 23.
steps.terutzMaskana: 'Went ahead' means he quickly declared he would pay.

steps.title: Renter says 'said,' borrower says 'went ahead'
steps.stepSummary: A wording difference between two ברייתות suggests that 'went ahead' means actual payment.
steps.simpleTranslation: But since the תנא says 'and he said' for a renter, and 'went ahead' for a borrower, learn from this that the wording is exact!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new challenge from wording. Another ברייתא uses different language for a renter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a renter, the ברייתא says 'and he said' (he would pay). For a borrower, it says 'went ahead.' If both meant 'said,' why change the words? The change suggests the borrower really must pay, as רב זביד said.

keyTerms.meaning: a renter (who pays to use the item)
a borrower (who uses it for free)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new opinion. It is a wording proof meant to show that 'went ahead' must mean actual payment.

phrases.english: But from the fact that it teaches 'and he said' regarding a renter,
phrases.notes: This is the renter ברייתא quoted back in step 13.

phrases.english: and 'went ahead' regarding a borrower,
learn from it that it teaches precisely!

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא מִדְּקָתָנֵי גַּבֵּי שׂוֹכֵר וְאָמַר וְגַבֵּי שׁוֹאֵל קִידֵּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the explanation in step 24 using a comparison with the renter ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The reading of 'קידם' as 'went ahead and said' (step 24)
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The renter ברייתא uses 'ואמר' while the borrower ברייתא uses 'קידם'. The different wording shows that 'קידם' means something else: actual payment.

steps.title: Maybe the two ברייתות were not taught together
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected, since separate ברייתות can simply use different styles.
steps.simpleTranslation: Were they taught next to each other?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the wording proof of step 25.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wording contrast only proves something if both lines come from the same source, taught side by side. The גמרא suggests these ברייתות may be separate, so each may just phrase things its own way. The next step checks whether this is true.

phrases.english: Are they taught next to each other?
phrases.notes: The גמרא is suggesting they might be two separate ברייתות, so a difference in wording would mean nothing. The next step checks this.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge brought in step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The wording inference from the renter and borrower ברייתות
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Wording differences are only meaningful in sources taught together. These two ברייתות may have been taught separately.

steps.title: The experts confirm the two teachings were taught together
steps.stepSummary: The reciters from the schools of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא say the two ברייתות were taught side by side as one teaching. This cancels the rejection in Step 26.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked the reciters of the schools of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא, and they said: these teachings are taught together.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא checks with the experts whether the two ברייתות really were separate. They answer that the ברייתות were one teaching recited together.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 said the wording difference meant nothing, because separate ברייתות can use different styles. Now we learn they were not separate; they were one teaching. So the change in wording is on purpose, and 'went ahead' really does seem to mean he actually paid. The challenge to רב פפא is back in force.

keyTerms.meaning: Here: the reciters who memorized ברייתות word for word
The school of רבי חייא, a main source of ברייתות

steps.confusionAlert: Here תנאי does not mean the great sages of the משנה era. It means the people in the study hall whose job was to memorize and recite ברייתות.

phrases.english: They asked the reciters
phrases.notes: These are the people who memorized ברייתות by heart, so they would know how the teachings were arranged.

phrases.aramaic: דְּבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּדְבֵי רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
phrases.english: of the school of Rabbi Chiyya and the school of Rabbi Oshaya
and they said: they are taught together.

steps.triggerLanguage: שַׁיְילִינְהוּ לְתַנָּאֵי דְּבֵי רַבִּי חִיָּיא וּדְבֵי רַבִּי אוֹשַׁעְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Overturns the rejection in Step 26 and restores the proof from Step 25.
steps.raayaObject: That the wording difference between the two ברייתות is meaningful, so 'went ahead' means actual payment
steps.raayaSupportSource: The testimony of the reciters of the schools of רבי חייא and רבי אושעיא that the ברייתות were taught together
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects Step 26's claim that the ברייתות were separate and could differ in style
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: Step 26 assumed the ברייתות were separate. In fact they were one combined teaching.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the גמרא can settle a question about how a teaching was worded by asking the people who preserved it, and not only by reasoning.

steps.title: Refusing and then agreeing to pay clearly counts
steps.stepSummary: Suppose a שומר first said 'I won't pay' and then said 'I will pay.' It is obvious he gets the כפל, because in the end he did say he would pay.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is obvious: if he said 'I will not pay' and then said 'I hereby pay,' he did say 'I hereby pay.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new topic: a שומר who changes his mind about paying. It starts with the easy case and says it needs no proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule is that a שומר who chooses to pay instead of swearing earns the כפל if the thief is found. If he refused at first but then agreed, his last statement is a willingness to pay. So he clearly qualifies. This easy case sets up the harder case that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: I hereby pay; I choose to pay
And he went back (changed his mind)

phrases.english: It is obvious:
if he said "I will not pay"
and then went back and said "I hereby pay"
after all, he did say "I hereby pay."

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא: אָמַר ״אֵינִי מְשַׁלֵּם״ וְחָזַר וְאָמַר ״הֲרֵינִי מְשַׁלֵּם״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new discussion built on רבי יוחנן's rule (step 10) that saying 'I will pay' is enough to earn the כפל.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A שומר who first refused but then agreed to pay gets the כפל, because his final statement is that he will pay.

steps.title: Starting the question about agreeing first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins to ask about the opposite order: what if he first said 'I will pay.'
steps.simpleTranslation: But if he said 'I hereby pay'...
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up the next question. Now the שומר agreed to pay first, and the rest of the question continues on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The easy case is settled. Now the גמרא turns the order around. Here the first statement is a willingness to pay, and the question is whether a later change of mind cancels it. The answer depends on what happens after this opening.

keyTerms.meaning: But; rather (it turns to the case that is really in doubt)
The double payment a thief must pay; the reward at stake for the שומר

phrases.english: But if he said "I hereby pay"
phrases.notes: The question isn't finished here; the rest of the case comes on the next amud.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the obvious case in Step 28 to the reverse case, which is in doubt.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a שומר who first said he would pay keeps the right to the כפל in the reverse case (the full question continues on the next amud).
